body:
The rise of regional kingdoms

Between the 7th and 15th centuries, political authority in western India was divided among several ruling families. Some controlled extensive kingdoms, while others exercised power over smaller regions. Their territories could expand or contract through warfare, alliances and changes in political loyalty.

Two important regional dynasties associated with medieval Gujarat were the Chavdas and the Chudasamas. Although their names are similar, they were different ruling families associated with different geographical centres.

Regional dynasty: A ruling family whose political authority was centred mainly on a particular region. A regional dynasty could be independent at one time and subordinate to a more powerful ruler at another.

Two distinct centres of political power

FeatureChavdasChudasamas
Principal regionNorth GujaratSaurashtra, especially Sorath
Important centresPanchasar and Anhilwad PatanVanthali and Junagadh
Important associationFoundation of Anhilwad PatanRule around Junagadh and Uparkot
Major political connectionSucceeded at Patan by the ChaulukyasContested power with the Chaulukyas and later the Gujarat Sultanate

Sorath refers to a historical region of Saurashtra, the peninsula in western Gujarat. It should not be confused with north Gujarat, where Anhilwad Patan became an important political centre.

Chronology and overlapping rule

The Chavdas are especially associated with the period from approximately the 8th to the mid-10th century. Their position at Patan was taken over by the Chaulukyas, also called Solankis, in the 10th century.

The early chronology of the Chudasamas is less certain. Traditions place their emergence in Saurashtra around the late 9th century. Their political history continued into the 15th century, when the Gujarat Sultanate defeated the ruling family at Junagadh in 1472 CE.

The chronology shows an important distinction: the Chudasamas did not simply replace the Chavdas. Their political centres were different, and Chudasama rule in Saurashtra overlapped with Chaulukya power in mainland Gujarat.

How regional rulers exercised authority

In early medieval India, powerful local chiefs were sometimes recognised as samantas, or subordinate rulers. They could provide military assistance and gifts to a more powerful king. When their resources and armed strength increased, some asserted greater independence.

Rulers depended on agricultural production, livestock, local trade and the support of influential families. Revenue helped maintain courts, soldiers, fortified settlements and religious institutions. Temples and towns could become centres of economic and cultural activity as well as places of worship.

This is the general pattern of regional government described for early medieval India. It does not mean that the Chavdas and Chudasamas possessed identical administrative systems or that every institution found in another dynasty existed under them.

Prelims focus

  • Chavdas: north Gujarat; Panchasar and Anhilwad Patan.
  • Chudasamas: Sorath in Saurashtra; Vanthali and Junagadh.
  • Chaulukya and Solanki are alternative names for the dynasty that succeeded the Chavdas at Patan.
  • Chudasama political history continued until the Gujarat Sultanate's conquest of Junagadh in 1472 CE.
  • Trap: Chavda and Chudasama are not alternative names for the same dynasty.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts–II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, printed pp. 16–21; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. I, Part I, History of Gujarat, 1896, Part II, Chapter I, sections 4–5; Samira Sheikh, Alliance, Genealogy and Political Power: The Cudasamas of Junagadh and the Sultans of Gujarat, The Medieval History Journal, Vol. 11, Issue 1, 2008, abstract; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Regional kingdoms developed around settlements, agriculture, trade and local centres of power.

title: The Chavdas and Chudasamas in Medieval Gujarat

body:
Panchasar and the early Chavda chiefs

The Chavdas, also written as Chavadas or Chapotkatas in historical accounts, were associated with Panchasar in north Gujarat before the rise of their capital at Anhilwad Patan. Panchasar lies in the region historically connected with the northern edge of Gujarat and the approaches towards Kachchh.

Traditional accounts name Jayashikhari as a Chavda chief of Panchasar and the father of Vanraj Chavda. They describe the loss of his kingdom and the subsequent rise of Vanraj. These stories preserve the connection between Panchasar and the later Chavda kingdom, although details of the early rulers and their dates are not uniformly established.

Vanraj Chavda and the foundation of Patan

Vanraj Chavda is the most important Chavda ruler for basic Gujarat history. He is traditionally credited with founding Anhilwad Patan, also called Anahilapura or Anhilpur Patan, and making it his capital.

The city was established in north Gujarat near the Saraswati River. A local tradition explains that Vanraj named it after his friend Anhil, described as a pastoralist in accounts of the city's foundation.

Establishing a capital gave the ruling family a recognised political centre. The court could operate from the city, military resources could be assembled there, and settlements associated with officials, traders, craftspeople and religious institutions could develop around it. Patan's importance continued long after the Chavdas ceased to rule.

A chronological distinction

The foundation of Anhilwad Patan is commonly placed around 745–746 CE, corresponding approximately to Vikram Samvat 802 in the traditional chronology. Published accounts are inconsistent. The Patan district's Culture and Heritage page gives 745 CE, while its English History page gives 802 CE. The latter should not be confused with Vikram Samvat 802, which falls in the 8th century CE. For the basic chronology, remember Vanraj's association with Patan and its foundation in approximately the mid-8th century rather than treating a disputed exact CE year as certain.

From the Chavdas to the Chaulukyas

The Chavdas continued to be associated with Anhilwad Patan until the mid-10th century. Traditional accounts identify Samantasimha as the last Chavda ruler at Patan.

Mulraja I established the rule of the Chaulukya or Solanki dynasty at Patan. Some traditional chronologies place this change around 942 CE, while historical reconstructions differ on the exact year. The secure political distinction is that the Chavda ruling family was replaced at Patan by the Chaulukyas during the 10th century.

This was a dynastic transition, not the foundation of an entirely new city by Mulraja. Patan remained an important capital under later Chaulukya rulers, including Bhima I, Siddharaja Jayasimha and Kumarapala.

The cultural importance of Patan

The Chavdas are principally remembered for the establishment of an important political centre. Much of Patan's best-known surviving monumental heritage belongs to the later Chaulukya period.

For example, Rani ki Vav at Patan is an 11th-century stepwell associated with the Chaulukya period. It should not be attributed to Vanraj Chavda merely because it stands in a city he is traditionally credited with founding.

This distinction helps separate the founding of a city from the construction of its later monuments. Several dynasties can contribute to the history of the same urban centre.

Prelims focus

  • Panchasar was an early centre associated with the Chavdas.
  • Jayashikhari is traditionally identified as Vanraj Chavda's father.
  • Vanraj Chavda is associated with the foundation of Anhilwad Patan in approximately the mid-8th century.
  • Traditional accounts connect Patan's name with Vanraj's friend Anhil.
  • Samantasimha is traditionally named as the last Chavda ruler at Patan.
  • Mulraja I established Chaulukya or Solanki rule at Patan in the 10th century.
  • Trap: Rani ki Vav belongs to the later Chaulukya period, not the Chavda foundation of Patan.

[Sources: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. I, Part I, History of Gujarat, 1896, Part II, Chapter I, sections 4–5 and 38–44; Government of Gujarat, Patan District Administration, History and Culture and Heritage pages; Government of Gujarat, NRI Division, Mehsana History, account of Vanraj and Mulraja; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, Brief Synthesis; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Authority moved from Panchasar to Anhilwad Patan, which remained a capital as Chavda rule gave way to Chaulukya rule.
pictures.caption: The capital survived a change of ruling dynasty.

title: The Chavdas: Panchasar, Vanraj and Anhilwad Patan

body:
The Chudasama kingdom in Saurashtra

The Chudasamas were a regional ruling family associated with Sorath in Saurashtra. Their important political centres included Vanthali, historically called Vamanasthali, and Junagadh, situated near the Girnar hills.

Unlike the Chavdas of Anhilwad Patan, the Chudasamas were primarily connected with the Saurashtra peninsula. Their rulers sometimes maintained local authority despite challenges from more powerful kingdoms based elsewhere in Gujarat.

Origins and chronology

Traditional accounts connect the Chudasamas with groups associated with Sindh and identify an early figure called Chudachandra. Their emergence in Saurashtra is often placed around the late 9th century. These accounts are not sufficiently consistent to establish an exact founding year or a complete sequence of early rulers.

The Chudasamas are commonly associated with the title Ra, used before the names of rulers in the Junagadh tradition. Thus, names such as Ra Navghan, Ra Khengar and Ra Mandalika refer to regional rulers; Ra is not a separate dynasty.

Important rulers and their political connections

Graharipu and Mulraja I

Graharipu was an early Chudasama ruler associated with Vanthali, generally placed in the 10th century. He is remembered for conflict with Mulraja I, the founder of Chaulukya rule at Patan.

Traditional Chaulukya accounts describe Mulraja's campaign against Graharipu and claim a victory over him. These accounts also connect the conflict with access to the pilgrimage centre of Somnath. The political relationship is important: it illustrates the attempt of a Patan-based ruler to extend influence into Saurashtra. The religious explanations in later royal narratives should not be treated as independently established motives for the war.

Ra Navghan and Junagadh

Ra Navghan is an important name in Chudasama traditions, especially those concerning the recovery or consolidation of power at Junagadh. An early Navghan is commonly associated with approximately the 11th century.

Accounts of his life contain legendary elements, and the name Navghan was used by more than one ruler. For basic chronology, his significance is the association with Chudasama power at Junagadh rather than a detailed biography or an exact reign length.

Ra Khengar and Siddharaja Jayasimha

Ra Khengar is remembered in connection with the struggle between the Chudasamas and Siddharaja Jayasimha, the Chaulukya ruler of Patan, during the 12th century.

Historical traditions describe Siddharaja's campaign against Khengar and the extension of Chaulukya control into Sorath. This was not a conflict between the Chavdas and Chudasamas: by Siddharaja's time, the Chaulukyas had long replaced the Chavdas at Patan.

Accounts of this conflict include the famous story of Ranakdevi. Its dramatic details belong to historical tradition and are not necessary for establishing the basic political sequence.

Ra Mandalika III and the Gujarat Sultanate

Ra Mandalika III was the important late Chudasama ruler associated with Junagadh in the mid-15th century. His reign marked the final phase of the dynasty's effective political independence.

In 1472 CE, the Chudasama ruler of Junagadh was defeated by the forces of Sultan Mahmud Begada of Gujarat. The conquest strengthened the Gujarat Sultanate's control over Saurashtra. The Chudasama ruling family lost its position as an independent regional power, although members of the family continued to hold local landed status.

Control over Sorath was contested. A Chudasama ruler's defeat by a Chaulukya king did not necessarily mean that the Chudasama ruling family disappeared permanently. The political history of Junagadh includes periods of local rule, external intervention and changing relationships with more powerful states.

Prelims focus

  • Chudasamas: Sorath in Saurashtra.
  • Vanthali or Vamanasthali: important early Chudasama centre.
  • Junagadh: major Chudasama centre near Girnar.
  • Graharipu is associated with conflict against Chaulukya Mulraja I.
  • Ra Khengar is associated with conflict against Chaulukya Siddharaja Jayasimha.
  • Ra Mandalika III is associated with the final phase of Chudasama rule at Junagadh.
  • Mahmud Begada's conquest of Junagadh is dated to 1472 CE.

[Sources: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. I, Part I, History of Gujarat, 1896, The Chudasamas, section 1, and The Chaulukyas, sections 16 and 23 and the section on Siddharaja Jayasimha; Samira Sheikh, State and Society in Gujarat, c. 1200–1500: The Making of a Region, University of Oxford, 2003, pp. 107–115; Samira Sheikh, Alliance, Genealogy and Political Power: The Cudasamas of Junagadh and the Sultans of Gujarat, The Medieval History Journal, Vol. 11, Issue 1, 2008, abstract; online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Junagadh's fortified landscape became an important centre of Chudasama power.

title: The Chudasamas of Sorath: Vanthali and Junagadh
